stem: A silver job receives one meter reading per row, and the device often sends NULL when a sensor skips a measurement. Analysts need every row to carry the most recent non-NULL `temp` of the same `device_id` at or before its `ts`. Which expression does this without a self-join?

choices.text: `last(temp, true) OVER (PARTITION BY device_id ORDER BY ts ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)`
`lag(temp, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY device_id ORDER BY ts)`, which returns the value of the previous row even when it is NULL
`max(temp) OVER (PARTITION BY device_id ORDER BY ts ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)` to carry the highest earlier value
`first_value(temp, true) OVER (PARTITION BY device_id ORDER BY ts ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)` to read the earliest non-NULL value

stem: A gold job needs one row per `sensor_id` that holds the three readings with the latest `ts` as an array. The team wants a single `GROUP BY sensor_id` aggregate, with no window function and no self-join. Which expression does this?

choices.text: `max_by(reading, ts)`, which returns the `reading` values of the three rows with the largest `ts` as an array
`max_by(reading, ts, 3)`, which returns an array with the readings of the three rows with the largest `ts`
`collect_list(reading)`, which returns the readings as an array sorted by `ts` from the newest to the oldest
`first(reading, 3)`, which returns the first three `reading` values of each group in arrival order

stem: A report uses `GROUP BY ROLLUP(region, channel)` and shows a row with `region = 'EU'` and `channel = NULL`. Some analysts read it as "EU sales with no channel recorded", but the source also contains genuine NULL channels. How should the query tell the subtotal row from real NULL data?

choices.text: Add `DISTINCT` to the select list, which removes the subtotal rows that repeat a region and leaves only the genuine NULL channels
Wrap `channel` in `coalesce(channel, 'ALL')`, which returns the label only for subtotal rows and never for source NULLs
Select `grouping(channel)` next to the columns; it is 1 for rows where `channel` was aggregated away and 0 for real values, including NULL
Replace `ROLLUP` with `GROUP BY region, channel` and add the totals later in a separate union with the same two columns

stem: Events were stored as JSON strings and queried with `payload:Customer_ID`. After the table was migrated to a VARIANT column built with `parse_json`, the same query returns NULL for every row, while the data still contains the key `customer_id`. What explains this?

choices.text: `parse_json` stores keys in alphabetical order and the engine matches by position, so a renamed key cannot be found
`parse_json` renames keys to lower case on conversion, so the query needs the stored key written in upper case instead
The `:` operator works only on STRING columns, so the query needs `get_json_object` over the column
VARIANT paths are case-sensitive, so `Customer_ID` and `customer_id` are different fields and the exact key is required

stem: A VARIANT column `raw` contains the key `zip.code`. The query `SELECT raw:`zip.code` FROM addresses` returns NULL for every row, although the key is present with values. Which change returns the values?

choices.text: Write `raw:['zip.code']`, because bracket notation escapes periods and square brackets in field names
Wrap the whole column in `to_json(raw)` and apply the colon operator to the resulting string
Cast the column first with `raw::string`, since VARIANT paths cannot contain periods before a cast
Write `raw:zip.code`, because the VARIANT operator takes a dotted name as one field key

stem: A VARIANT column `payload` holds an order with an array `items` of objects such as `{"sku":"A1","qty":2}`. A fact table needs one row per item with `sku` and `qty` as typed columns. Which query builds it?

choices.text: `SELECT o.id, explode(o.payload:items) FROM orders o`, because the generic function is the only one that unpacks arrays
`SELECT o.id, payload:items[*].sku FROM orders o`, which expands all array elements into separate rows
`SELECT o.id, i.value:sku::string AS sku, i.value:qty::int AS qty FROM orders o, LATERAL variant_explode(o.payload:items) i`
`SELECT o.id, payload:items:sku::string FROM orders o GROUP BY o.id`, which flattens the array while grouping by order

stem: A bronze table stores webhook bodies from 30 partners as VARIANT. Before promoting stable fields into typed silver columns, the team wants one summary of the combined structure and types seen across the whole column, including fields that appear only in some rows. Which function fits?

choices.text: `schema_of_json_agg(payload)`, which accepts VARIANT input and merges the field types of every row
`schema_of_variant(payload)` applied to the first row only, since one row always holds all possible fields
`payload::string` followed by a `DESCRIBE` of the table, because the metadata lists the nested fields of VARIANT columns
`schema_of_variant_agg(payload)`, which merges the schemas of all rows and falls back to VARIANT for conflicting types

stem: A nightly ingest runs `SELECT parse_json(body) AS v FROM bronze_raw`. One partner occasionally sends truncated JSON and the whole job fails. Bad rows must be kept for inspection, and good rows must flow. What is the best design?

choices.text: Keep `parse_json` and set `failOnError => false` on the call so that the failed rows come back as error messages for review
Use `try_parse_json(body)`, which returns NULL on invalid JSON, and route NULL results with non-NULL input to a rejects table
Cast with `body::variant`, which silently converts malformed JSON text to a VARIANT string value
Wrap the call in `ai_query` to repair broken JSON before parsing, so that no row ever fails

stem: A VARIANT column `v` holds events like `{"id":1,"coupon":null}` and `{"id":2}`. A data quality check must count events where the key `coupon` is present with an explicit JSON null, separately from events without the key. Which predicates separate the two cases?

choices.text: `try_variant_get(v, '$.coupon', 'string') IS NULL` is true only for the explicit null and false for a key that is missing
`v:coupon = 'null'` is true for the explicit null, while a missing key returns the string `'missing'`
`v:coupon IS NULL` is true for both cases, so the cases cannot be told apart in SQL at all
`is_variant_null(v:coupon)` is true when the key holds an explicit null, while `v:coupon IS NULL` is true when the key is missing

stem: A team wants to enable VARIANT on an existing Delta table that is also read by an external engine using a Delta Lake reader library. What must the team consider before running `ALTER TABLE ... SET TBLPROPERTIES('delta.feature.variantType' = 'supported')`?

choices.text: Enabling it upgrades the table writer protocol, which can break external Delta clients without support for it
The feature can be enabled only when the table is created, so an existing table must be recreated from scratch
VARIANT requires converting the table to Iceberg v2 first, because Delta tables cannot store any kind of semi-structured data type
The command rewrites all data files into a new layout, so the table is unavailable until the rewrite completes

stem: A compliance team must be able to prove the exact text of every webhook body received. The bronze table stores `body` as STRING and a derived column `v = parse_json(body)`. An engineer proposes to drop `body` and keep only `v`, converting back with `to_json(v)` when needed. What is the problem?

choices.text: VARIANT values are stored as compressed archives that cannot be read after 30 days, so the raw text must be kept
`parse_json` is not exactly reversible: whitespace, key order and trailing zeros are not preserved, so keep the raw text
`to_json` cannot convert a VARIANT value back to text, so the conversion is not available at all
The conversion only changes the data type, so the proposal is safe and the original text can be rebuilt byte for byte from the stored VARIANT value

stem: A batch enrichment job runs `SELECT id, ai_query('databricks-llama', 'Summarize: ' || text) AS summary FROM tickets` over 8 million rows. A few hundred rows hit endpoint errors, and the entire query fails and discards hours of work. The team wants the other rows to complete and the failures to be retried later. What should change?

choices.text: Wrap the call in `try_cast`, which turns any endpoint error into NULL before it can fail the query
Switch the table to a provisioned throughput endpoint, which never returns row-level errors
Add `failOnError => false`; each result becomes a struct with response and error message, so failed rows can be selected and retried later
Split the table into thousands of small queries run one after another, so that an endpoint error only hits a small part of the data

stem: A pipeline runs `ai_query` over 50 million documents once a day. An engineer proposes to chunk the table into 5,000-row slices in a Python loop and call the function per slice, to "protect the endpoint". What is the better design?

choices.text: Collect the documents to the driver and call the model serving REST API with a thread pool for full control
Use a provisioned throughput endpoint for the batch, because pay-per-token endpoints cannot serve batch queries from SQL
Keep the loop, but add a sleep between slices, because AI Functions cannot run in parallel on a cluster
Send the whole dataset in one query to a Databricks-hosted foundation model endpoint and let AI Functions parallelize and retry

stem: A pipeline uses `ai_query` to extract `vendor`, `total` and `due_date` from invoice text. The current prompt asks for JSON and a downstream `from_json` step fails on about 3% of rows because the model adds explanatory text. Which change makes the output reliably parseable?

choices.text: Lower the model temperature to zero in `modelParameters`, which guarantees that the model returns valid JSON every time
Add a second `ai_query` call that asks the model to check whether its first answer was valid JSON
Pass a `responseFormat` with a JSON schema or DDL schema, so the chat model must return output that follows it
Apply `regexp_extract` to remove all text before the first brace, which works for any model output

stem: A platform team wants analysts to run ready-made text classification and translation, while data engineers can also run custom prompts against chosen models in pipelines. How do the two kinds of AI Functions differ?

choices.text: Task-specific functions require the engineer to create a model serving endpoint first, while `ai_query` needs no endpoint
Task-specific functions such as `ai_translate` cover one task; `ai_query` is the general-purpose function for custom prompts and models
`ai_query` is limited to traditional ML endpoints, while task-specific functions are the only route to a large language model
Task-specific functions run only on classic SQL warehouses, while `ai_query` runs only on serverless compute and notebooks

stem: A governance team removed `EXECUTE` on the `system.ai` schema from all users and granted it back for only `ai_translate` and `ai_summarize`. Analysts can still run `ai_query` against a hosted foundation model. Why?

choices.text: These permissions do not govern `ai_query`, which calls a serving endpoint, so endpoint permissions control it
`ai_query` is exempt only for users with workspace admin rights, and the analysts are admins
The privilege change is cached for 24 hours, so `ai_query` is blocked only after the metastore has refreshed its privileges
Revoking `EXECUTE` on a schema affects only SQL warehouses, and analysts use notebooks on classic clusters

stem: Finance asks which jobs spend the most on LLM calls made with `ai_query` against Databricks-hosted foundation model endpoints. Where should the data engineer look?

choices.text: In the compute metrics of the job cluster, because the inference runs on the same cluster that submits the query
In `system.billing.usage` records with product `MODEL_SERVING` and offering type `BATCH_INFERENCE`, joined to job metadata
In `system.billing.usage` records with product `AI_FUNCTIONS`, since `ai_query` is always recorded under that product
Only in the Spark UI of each job, because AI Function costs are not stored in system tables

stem: An engineer wants to give each row its own output limit: `modelParameters => named_struct('max_tokens', t.limit_tokens)`, where `limit_tokens` is a column, and the query is rejected. What is the rule?

choices.text: Model parameters are ignored unless `failOnError` is set to false, so the engineer must enable it first
Model parameters are accepted only for custom model endpoints, and a hosted foundation model needs the limit in the prompt text
Model parameters must be constant values and cannot depend on row data, so use a fixed value or run separate queries per limit
The struct must be passed through `responseFormat`, which is the only argument that accepts column references

stem: A job must describe product photos stored as files in a Unity Catalog volume with a hosted vision model. The folder contains JPEG, PNG and TIFF files. Which approach fits the multimodal support of `ai_query`?

choices.text: Read with `read_files` as `binaryFile`, pass `files => content`, and convert TIFF files to JPEG or PNG first
Use `files => path`, because the parameter takes the file location and reads any format
Base64-encode every file in a UDF and concatenate it into the prompt, which works for all formats
Pass the file path strings in the prompt text, because the endpoint downloads the images from the Unity Catalog volume itself

stem: A streaming table receives trip records. Rows with a NULL pickup or dropoff zip must not reach the gold reports, but compliance requires keeping them for review with the reason. Which design in a Lakeflow pipeline meets both needs?

choices.text: A plain `expect` on one table, since invalid rows are automatically written to a separate quarantine table
`expect_or_drop` on the zip rules; the dropped count in the metrics is enough to review the cases
`expect_or_fail` on the zip rules, so that any invalid trip stops the whole update until someone fixes the source data
Add an `is_quarantined` flag in a table with `expect_all`, then expose valid and invalid rows as two views

stem: A triggered pipeline has a validation materialized view with `expect_or_fail("unique_pk", "num_entries = 1")` that checks the primary key of the `report` table. A violation is found, the validation flow fails, yet the downstream `report_export` table updated successfully with the duplicates. What explains this?

choices.text: Only that flow is rolled back in a triggered pipeline; a validation table does not gate other tables, which update on their own
Fail expectations apply only to streaming tables, so the materialized view only warned and recorded the violation metrics instead of failing
The pipeline needs a continuous mode to evaluate expectations, and a triggered update skips them
The failure is retried in the background, and `report_export` read the data before the retry finished

stem: A continuous pipeline contains a streaming table `payments_clean` with `expect_or_fail("positive_amount", "amount > 0")`, which feeds three downstream tables. One bad record arrives. What is the result, and what must the team do?

choices.text: The flow pauses for one minute and then resumes automatically with the bad record written to the target
Only the failing flow stops, while the three downstream tables keep updating from data already in `payments_clean`
The flow and its dependent flows stop and the pipeline reports why; the code must be fixed before restart
Only the bad record is skipped and the stream continues, and the team reviews the dropped count later

stem: An `expect_or_fail("temperature_in_valid_range", "temperature BETWEEN -50 AND 60")` stops an update. The engineer must find which input record broke it. Where is that information, and which statement about metrics is true?

choices.text: The event log never has information for failures, so the engineer must rerun the pipeline with debug logging
The failing record is written to a quarantine table automatically, and the update is partly committed
Only the Data quality tab lists the failing record, and it shows a count of failed records for fail actions
The failure message names the expectation and shows the records in many queries; fail actions record no metrics

stem: A data platform team maintains the same 8 data quality rules for 25 Python datasets in several pipelines. Rules change monthly, and auditors want rule changes recorded without editing pipeline code. What is the recommended structure?

choices.text: Define the rules in a SQL file and read them with a dynamic expectation clause, which SQL expectations support
Keep the rules in a tagged Delta table, load them into a dictionary and pass it to `expect_all_or_drop`
Copy the rule strings into each dataset decorator, so that every pipeline stays self-contained and reviewable alone
Set the rules as pipeline configuration parameters and expect the engine to apply them to all datasets automatically

stem: A silver streaming table must keep every record for a new data source while analysts learn how bad the data is. After a month the team wants to start removing the invalid records. How should the actions be sequenced?

choices.text: Start with plain `expect` to keep rows and collect metrics, then switch stable rules to `expect_or_drop`
Start with `expect_or_drop` and rebuild dropped rows from the event log whenever analysts need them
Start with `expect_or_fail` so that bad data never lands in the table, then relax to `drop` once the data is clean
Start without expectations and add them only at the gold layer, where invalid rows cannot affect metrics

stem: An engineer defines a streaming table in a standalone pipeline created in Databricks SQL with `CONSTRAINT valid_amount EXPECT (amount > 0) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW`, and looks for the Data quality tab in the pipeline UI. The tab is missing. Where can the expectation metrics be read?

choices.text: In the query history of the SQL warehouse, which stores the number of dropped rows per statement
By querying the pipeline event log, since the Data quality tab is unavailable for standalone SQL pipelines
Only in the table history of the target table, where the dropped count is shown as an operation metric of each write
Nowhere, because expectations on Databricks SQL streaming tables do not record any metrics at all

stem: A pipeline uses an AUTO CDC FROM SNAPSHOT flow to maintain a dimension from periodic snapshots. The team adds an expectation to the flow's target definition and gets no enforcement and no metrics. What is the right way to validate the dimension?

choices.text: Add the expectation as a SQL comment, which Lakeflow Pipelines read as a data quality rule
Increase the snapshot frequency, because expectations evaluate only when two snapshots differ by at least one changed row
Put the expectation on a downstream dataset that reads the dimension, since this flow does not support expectations
Convert the flow to a standard append flow, which is the only flow type that can write the dimension

stem: A team writes its pipelines in SQL and wants to apply one shared set of 10 rules with a single drop action to 30 tables, the way Python authors use `expect_all_or_drop` with a dictionary. What is true for SQL datasets?

choices.text: SQL expectations cannot drop rows, so a shared drop action must be implemented in a Python dataset that reads the SQL output
SQL has an `EXPECT ALL` clause that reads a rules table by tag, which is the SQL equivalent of the Python dictionary helper
SQL supports only one expectation per dataset, so the 10 rules must be combined into a single boolean expression joined with `AND`
Grouping rules with a collective action is Python only; in SQL each rule is its own `CONSTRAINT ... EXPECT ... ON VIOLATION DROP ROW` clause

stem: A streaming table in a pipeline has `expect_or_drop` rules. An engineer sums the expectation counts from `flow_progress` event log rows whose status is `COMPLETED` and gets no counts for some updates, although rows were dropped. Which change finds the counts?

choices.text: Query the Delta history of the target table, where each streaming write stores the dropped-row count
Switch the rules to `expect_or_fail`, because fail actions record the complete expectation metrics in the final event of every update, even when the update itself fails
Run a full refresh of the table, which rewrites the metrics into the `COMPLETED` event of the update
Also read the `flow_progress` events with status `RUNNING`, because for some flows the metrics are reported per micro-batch there
